title: Continuous-wave AC magnetometry up to hundreds of megahertz using nitrogen-vacancy centers under a strong transverse magnetic field
authors: Ryusei Okaniwa, Rui Suzuki, Yuichiro Matsuzaki, Norio Tokuda, Junko Ishi-Hayase
abstract: Nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centers in diamond are promising quantum sensors for AC magnetic fields. However, conventional dynamical-decoupling-based magnetometry becomes technically demanding at high frequencies because of the requirement for increasingly short and high-power microwave pulses. This paper describes an AC magnetometry technique based on continuous-wave optically detected magnetic resonance (CW-ODMR) measurements, which enables the detection of signals in the hundred-MHz range. By applying a strong static magnetic field transverse to the NV axis, the energy separation between the relevant electron-spin states was tuned and resonantly coupled with the target radiofrequency (RF) magnetic field, thereby forming RF-dressed states. Unlike pulsed dynamical-decoupling schemes, this approach does not require high-power microwave pulse sequences. The key feature of our method is that the detectable frequency can be tuned by controlling the bias magnetic field strength. Using this methodology, we have experimentally achieved the frequency-tunable detection of AC magnetic fields from 14.4-632 MHz. The sensitivity was 0.558 uT/Hz^(0.5) at 14.4 MHz and 24.4 uT/Hz^(0.5) at 632 MHz. We characterized the field-dependent ODMR contrast and linewidth, and found that their degradation at large transverse fields is a important factor limiting the high-frequency sensitivity. These results establish a simple CW-ODMR approach for widely tunable RF magnetic-field sensing without high-power pulsed spin control.
summary: This paper introduces a novel, continuous-wave technique for AC magnetometry using NV centers in diamond, circumventing the need for high-power microwave pulses. By applying a strong transverse magnetic field, the system forms tunable RF-dressed states, enabling the detection of magnetic fields up to hundreds of MHz. This establishes a simple, widely tunable quantum sensing method for magnetic field measurements.
main_problem: To develop a high-frequency AC magnetometry technique using Nitrogen-Vacancy (NV) centers that avoids the technical difficulties associated with high-power microwave pulses.
main_result: The authors successfully demonstrated frequency-tunable detection of AC magnetic fields across a wide range (14.4–632 MHz) using a continuous-wave optically detected magnetic resonance (CW-ODMR) approach.
method: The technique relies on creating RF-dressed states by applying a strong static transverse magnetic field ($B_x$) to tune the energy separation between NV electron spin states, allowing detection via CW-ODMR.
model_or_system: The physical system is the NV center in diamond, whose electron spin Hamiltonian is analyzed. The method involves diagonalizing the total Hamiltonian, which includes terms for strain, static magnetic fields, and the applied microwave/RF driving fields.
key_observables: AC magnetic field frequency range (14.4–632 MHz), sensitivity ($\mu	ext{T}/\sqrt{	ext{Hz}}$), ODMR contrast, and linewidth.
important_parameters: Strong transverse magnetic field ($B_x$), bias magnetic field strength, and the frequency range of the target AC field.
main_assumptions: The method is limited by the degradation of ODMR contrast and linewidth at large transverse fields, which is a key factor limiting high-frequency sensitivity.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the energy level diagrams showing the formation of RF-dressed states, the spectral dips observed under RF irradiation, and the dependence of sensitivity on the bias field strength.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from identifying the limitations of pulsed magnetometry to proposing the CW-ODMR approach. It details the theoretical framework involving Hamiltonian diagonalization, presents experimental measurements across a wide frequency range, and analyzes the sources of sensitivity degradation.
why_interesting: This work provides a robust, non-pulsed quantum sensing platform for magnetic fields, directly relevant to open quantum systems and quantum optics by utilizing coherent control (dressing) in a solid-state solid-state quantum sensor.
